text: With Redis, overwriting a key with SET clears its TTL. Write SET key value EX 30 (or SET followed by EXPIRE) on every heartbeat, or the key never expires. Since Redis 2.6 the expiry error is 0-1 ms.
why: The obvious implementation (plain SET) silently breaks the design.

text: DynamoDB TTL deletes expired items 'typically within a few days', and until then they are still returned by reads. Store an epoch-seconds expiry attribute and treat expiry < now as offline (use filter expressions on Query and Scan).
why: Without this, DynamoDB would show users online for hours after they left.

text: Redis expires keys two ways: passively, when a client accesses an expired key, and actively, by periodically testing random keys that have a TTL and deleting expired ones.
why: Explains why TTL deletion is cheap for Redis.

text: DynamoDB TTL deletions do not consume write throughput, and they appear in DynamoDB Streams as service deletions, distinct from user deletes. An archival consumer can therefore tell expiries apart from explicit deletes.
why: Directly supports the TTL-plus-streams archival idea discussed.

text: Debezium's MySQL connector reads the MySQL binlog and produces row-level change events that it publishes to Kafka topics.
why: Shows how CDC replaces DynamoDB Streams on MySQL.

text: PostgreSQL's INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE is an atomic upsert: it inserts the row or updates the existing one, even under high concurrency. It covers the first heartbeat of a user with no row yet.
why: A plain UPDATE misses users who have no row yet.

text: A 4-byte epoch-seconds timestamp runs out in 2038: MySQL's TIMESTAMP type has a range of '1970-01-01 00:00:01' to '2038-01-19 03:14:07' UTC. New schemas should use 8-byte timestamps.
why: The 4+4 byte estimate hides the Year-2038 limit.

text: Each PostgreSQL row carries a fixed 23-byte header plus a 4-byte item pointer in its page, so an 8-byte payload row takes about 40 bytes on disk before indexes.
why: Calibrates back-of-envelope storage estimates.

text: The official redis-benchmark output shows about 180,000 SET requests/s on one instance without pipelining, and over 1.5 million/s with 16-command pipelining. 100k heartbeats/s is within one Redis node's range.
why: Gives a real number for the 6M/min (100k/s) write load.

text: HikariCP's connectionTimeout (default 30 s) is how long a caller waits for a free pooled connection before getting an error. maximumPoolSize (default 10) caps idle plus in-use connections.
why: Concrete defaults for the min/max/wait behaviour taught.

text: HikariCP's idleTimeout (default 10 minutes) retires idle connections, but only when minimumIdle is below maximumPoolSize. maxLifetime (default 30 minutes) retires every connection after a fixed age.
why: Matches the teacher's 10-minute example and separates idle timeout from max lifetime.

text: HikariCP recommends not setting minimumIdle, so the pool acts as a fixed-size pool (minimum = maximum); its default minimumIdle equals maximumPoolSize.
why: A widely used pool's guidance contrasts with 'start with 3-5'.

text: HikariCP's pool-sizing guide suggests connections = ((core_count * 2) + effective_spindle_count) as a starting point. It warns that beyond the optimum, throughput falls and response times climb.
why: Shows why a bigger pool is not the cure for slower queries.

text: Amazon RDS Proxy and PgBouncer sit between app servers and the database and pool connections centrally. RDS Proxy queues or throttles client connections it cannot serve immediately, protecting the database from oversubscription during traffic surges.
why: The standard fix for 'pool minimum x servers exceeds the DB limit'.

text: On RDS the default max_connections is computed from instance memory: MySQL {DBInstanceClassMemory/12582880} (about MB/12; about 630 on an 8 GiB db.m7g.large), PostgreSQL LEAST({DBInstanceClassMemory/9531392}, 5000).
why: Gives the actual formula the teacher mentions.

text: PostgreSQL uses a process-per-connection model: for every new connection request the postmaster spawns a new backend process.
why: Names the real database-side cost of a new connection.

text: An AWS Application Load Balancer health-checks each target every 30 s by default and takes it out of service after 2 consecutive failures (5 successes to bring it back).
why: Shows the pull-based form of the same failure detection, with real defaults.

text: Facebook Messenger keeps a persistent connection to Facebook's servers using MQTT, a protocol chosen to avoid draining phone batteries.
why: A real-world example of the persistent-connection approach.

text: PostgreSQL's max_connections defaults to typically 100, and superuser_reserved_connections (default 3) are held back for administrators, so applications get fewer than max_connections.
why: Refines the per-server pool maximum calculation.

text: EC2 limits how many connections can be tracked per instance; beyond the limit packets are dropped. The conntrack_allowance_exceeded metric shows it, and with load balancers AWS recommends scaling instance count or size.
why: The actual network-side limit on connection counts.

text: Redis has been benchmarked at more than 60,000 client connections while sustaining 50,000 queries/s. As a rule of thumb, 30,000 connections yield about half the throughput of 100.
why: Answers the 'how does a server hold 30k+ connections' question with data.

text: WebSocket (RFC 6455) gives a client and server two-way communication over one connection. Before it, getting server updates meant polling the server over HTTP.
why: Names the protocol behind the board's 'unless there is a persistent connection'.
